name: Hong Kong-Macau Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Sign language; word stress inapplicable and no stress description exists; MEDs (Tang 2007 etc.) are sign phonology.

sources.citation: Tang, Gladys. 2015. Hong Kong Sign Language. In William S-Y. Wang & Chaofen Sun (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Chinese Linguistics, 710-728. Oxford: Oxford University Press. DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199856336.013.0062
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Phonology section (54.3.1, pp. 716-717) lists contrastive handshapes, palm orientations, locations and movements and Mak & Tang's movement types; the only prosody remark (p. 725) is that 'cues such as eye blinks and head nods occur usually at the right edge of phonological or intonational phrases'; the words stress/prominence/accent never occur.

sources.citation: Sze, Felix. 2004. Blinks and intonational phrases in Hong Kong Sign Language. Paper presented at TISLR 8, Barcelona (published 2008 as 'Blinks and intonational phrasing in Hong Kong Sign Language', in J. Quer (ed.), Signs of the Time: Selected papers from TISLR 2004, 83-107. Hamburg: Signum)
sources.note: Phrase-level only: blinks are classified against syntactic/intonational boundaries; on stress it says only that HKSL lexical (Type IV) blinks 'may emphasize the meaning of the co-occurring lexical items but are restricted to certain linguistic contexts. In other words, Type IV blinks do not seem to perform a general function of marking emphasis or stress' (sec. 6, Conclusion). No statement on where word stress falls.

sources.citation: Siu, Wai Yan Rebecca. 2016. Sociolinguistic Variation in Hong Kong Sign Language. PhD thesis, Victoria University of Wellington. DOI 10.26686/wgtn.17020070
sources.note: Lexical and phonological (location-drop) variation; 'stress' occurs only in non-linguistic senses; silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Tang, Gladys, Jia Li, Felix Sze, Jafi Lee, Joe Mak Ka-Leong, Kenny Chu, Brenda Yu, Aaron Wong & Connie Lo. 2025. Hong Kong Sign Language. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. ISBN 9781501516849, 350 pp.

sources.note: Google Books snippets: sign languages 'prefer prominence in phrase-final position (Wilbur 1997; Nespor & Sandler 1999)' and 'stressed signs (or signs in focus) [are] produced in phrase-final position'; HKSL is named only for blinks that 'consistently occur at intonational phrase boundaries' (citing Tang et al. 2010). General/second-hand, not an HKSL word-stress statement.
